summary: Gives recommendations for switches that snoop on IGMP and MLD messages to work out which ports need which multicast traffic. It builds on best current practice for IGMPv2, with extra considerations for IGMPv3 and MLDv2 snooping and for link-layer topology changes. This is informational guidance.

plainLanguage.summary: A mail room could copy a newsletter to every desk, or only to people who signed up. This memo explains how a switch listens in to learn who signed up so it delivers multicast traffic only there.

subtitle: How switches can learn multicast group membership to avoid wasting bandwidth.

tldr.problem: Without multicast group membership awareness, network switches flood multicast packets to all ports, wasting bandwidth on segments where no host needs the traffic.
tldr.mechanism: A snooping switch passively listens to IGMP (for IPv4) and MLD (for IPv6) membership reports to learn which ports have members of which groups, then forwards multicast traffic only to interested ports.
tldr.outcome: Bandwidth is conserved on network segments with no listeners, while ensuring group members still receive their traffic. This enables efficient multicast deployment in switched networks.

today: RFC 4541 remains the authoritative guidance for IGMP and MLD snooping implementations. It has not been obsoleted, and its recommendations continue to be widely followed by switch vendors. The prevalence of multicast in modern networks—for IPTV, video conferencing, and other applications—makes snooping switches essential for efficient bandwidth utilization.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
In a traditional network switch, multicast packets destined to a group address are forwarded to all ports on all segments, following standard IEEE bridging rules. This ensures all group members receive the traffic, but wastes bandwidth on segments where no host has interest in the group. For networks with heavy multicast load, this flooding can impact performance and prevent other traffic from being sent.

An IGMP snooping switch improves on this by examining IGMP membership reports to learn which ports have active receivers for each group, then forwarding multicast data only to those ports and to ports where multicast routers are attached. This document provides recommendations for implementing IGMP and MLD snooping switches, built on best current practice and vendor experience.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of sending a package to every address, a mail carrier asks who wants it, then delivers only there. A snooping switch eavesdrops on those requests.

sections.title: IGMP Forwarding and Router Detection
sections.content:
A snooping switch must maintain a list of multicast router ports and forward IGMP Membership Reports only to those ports, not to regular host ports. This prevents hosts from receiving membership reports from other hosts, which can cause suppression of their own reports in IGMPv1 and IGMPv2 (where one report can silence others).

The switch can build the router port list by listening for IGMP Queries from non-zero source addresses, by accepting Multicast Router Advertisement messages, or through explicit administrative configuration. The switch must also recognize unregistered IGMP messages and forward them to all ports without modification, preserving compatibility with different IGMP versions. Special handling is required when different IGMP versions coexist: an IGMPv3 snooping switch must recognize IGMPv3 query format despite using the same message type number as older versions.
sections.plainLanguage: The switch must know where the routers are, separate membership reports from regular traffic, and handle different IGMP versions gracefully.

sections.title: Multicast Data Forwarding Rules
sections.content:
For data packets, the core rule is: forward multicast packets matching known group memberships only to ports that requested those groups, plus all router ports. Packets with unregistered group addresses (not seen in any membership report) should be forwarded to all router ports so routers can manage the source. Link-local addresses (224.0.0.X in IPv4) receive special handling: many applications do not send IGMP joins for these addresses, so they should be flooded to all ports to avoid breaking legacy services.

A snooping switch should use IP address-based forwarding rather than media access control (MAC) address forwarding when possible, because each Ethernet multicast MAC address in IPv4 can correspond to 32 different IP group addresses, creating ambiguity. The switch must verify IP header checksums before incorporating packet information into forwarding tables, and must implement membership timeout mechanisms so group entries do not remain indefinitely after hosts leave.
sections.plainLanguage: Send multicast only where it was requested, but flood link-local traffic and unknown senders to routers. Use IP addresses, not MAC addresses, to track groups.

sections.title: IGMPv3 Support and Source-Based Filtering
sections.content:
IGMPv3 introduces source-based filtering: hosts can ask for traffic from specific sources (INCLUDE lists) or specifically exclude certain sources (EXCLUDE lists). A snooping switch receiving IGMPv3 include-source and exclude-source membership reports must forward the superset of all reports on a shared segment, computing whether traffic from a particular source to a particular group should be forwarded based on all hosts' include and exclude lists combined.

A challenge arises when IGMPv2 snooping switches operate alongside IGMPv3 routers and hosts: the switch will not recognize IGMPv3 membership reports and cannot properly forward traffic, potentially breaking services or causing excessive flooding. The recommendation is to configure the router to operate in IGMPv2 mode, or disable IGMP snooping entirely if v3 compatibility cannot be achieved. Ideally, snooping switches should at least recognize IGMPv3 joins and treat them like IGMPv2 joins by forwarding the group without source filtering.
sections.plainLanguage: Newer IGMP can ask for traffic from only certain sources. Switches must handle this carefully and work with both old and new versions without breaking.

sections.title: IPv6 Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD)
sections.content:
MLD serves the same role for IPv6 as IGMP does for IPv4. The control and data forwarding rules are largely the same, with a few differences: IPv6 MLD messages use ICMPv6 message types rather than separate IGMP messages, so a snooping switch must carefully distinguish MLD messages from other ICMPv6 traffic to avoid overloading the CPU with irrelevant packets. Additionally, IPv6 multicast addresses have a different structure and can map to many more IP addresses per MAC address (over 10^24 compared to 32 for IPv4), making IP address-based forwarding strongly preferred.

The address FF02::1 (all-hosts link-scope) receives special handling: MLD messages are never sent for this address, so switches should forward such traffic to all ports. Addresses in the range FF00::/15 should never appear on the link and require no state. As with IPv4, the switch must not reject MLD reports due to unspecified source addresses (::), and must use the null IP source address when spoofing queries during topology changes.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 uses MLD instead of IGMP, with the same idea but different message formats. IPv6 addresses create more ambiguity, so IP-based forwarding is even more important.

sections.title: Spanning Tree Integration and Interoperability
sections.content:
When a switch's spanning tree algorithm enables or disables a port, the topology changes and group membership state may need to be refreshed. A non-querier snooping switch should send a general IGMP or MLD query on all active non-router ports to speed network convergence, but must use a zero source address (0.0.0.0 or ::) to indicate that the query is not from a multicast router, preventing the switch from being elected as Querier. These proxy queries must not participate in Querier election.

The document emphasizes robust error handling: switches must not incorporate information from IGMP or MLD packets with checksum errors, and must gracefully handle multicast packets from sources not in the 0.0.0.X range. By providing clear recommendations for these scenarios, the RFC enables switches from different vendors to coexist and interoperate reliably in multicast networks.
sections.plainLanguage: When the network topology changes, the switch might need to refresh who wants what multicast traffic. It must do this carefully without disrupting the election of routers.

left.title: Traditional Switch
left.desc: Forwards multicast to every port regardless of interest.

right.title: Snooping Switch
right.desc: Learns group membership and forwards only where needed.
